text: Right-sizing means matching an EC2 instance's size to what it actually uses, not what seemed like a cautious, safe guess back at launch time. It's extremely common for an instance to get launched a size or two larger than it truly needs, and then never get revisited again once it's quietly running in production.

The signal worth checking is CloudWatch's CPUUtilization metric, along with memory usage, averaged over a couple of weeks of real traffic rather than a single snapshot. An instance that never breaks 10 to 15% CPU, even during its own peak traffic, is a strong candidate to downsize to a smaller instance type in the same family — same capability the workload actually uses, noticeably lower hourly cost.

Terminating an EC2 instance doesn't always terminate its attached EBS volume along with it. A volume that isn't set to delete on termination gets left behind, unattached, quietly billing by the gigabyte-month for absolutely nothing useful. This CLI call lists every volume currently sitting in the available state — meaning not attached to any instance at all — which is exactly the list worth reviewing on a schedule and cleaning up.

Old EBS snapshots accumulate the same quiet way volumes do; a sensible retention policy that keeps only the last several and automatically drops the rest closes that particular gap. S3 lifecycle policies solve the equivalent problem for objects instead, automatically aging data down from Standard into Standard-IA, then into Glacier, then Glacier Deep Archive, and deleting it outright once it passes its defined retention window.

An m5.xlarge running under 8% CPU and under 30% memory, even at its own peak, clearly never needed four vCPUs in the first place. Resizing it down to an m5.large roughly halves the hourly compute cost while still leaving comfortable headroom to spare.
